My set up is basically three separate units. The first two units are a fire two fire brick ovens.

One fire brick oven has a oven over the fire box. The hot gases from the burning fuel (I use dried sage brush) heat the bottom, sides and back of the oven box before escaping out the top. The door to the oven is a heavy gauge cast iron with a asbestos rope as the gasket. All the hot gasses from the wood being turned into charcoal are captured and distilled in a cold water bath. This gives me pure charcoal as well as creosote, Methanol , turpentine, and other stuff. The oven box is about 18 inches by 18 inches by 18 inches. I originally built a bigger one built loardy it took a lot of fuel to make the charcoal.

The second fire brick unit is my smelter. With high pressure air being forced through the bottom and along the lower sides I can get it up to 3500 Fahrenheit with no sweat. I run it at about 30 PSI from a 5 hp Air Compressor. The fire box is again 18 inches by 18 inches by 18 inches. I generally run two (4 by 10 by 4 ceramic crucibles) for smelting of metal. You have to be careful with the ceramic crucibles because if you take them out of a hot smelter and place them on a cold surface they will break. If you have time it is best to let them cool in the smelter. To remove the metal turn them upside down on a metal rack and heat them evenly with a acetylene torch. This causes the crucible to expand and break loose from the metal inside.

The last unit is my forge. it is a welded metal box about 2 feet three inches long by 21 inches wide and a foot high mounted on a 4 inch double extra heavy black iron pipe. The reason for the wierd measments is the forge is lined with 3 inch thick fire brick, so the forge is two feet long by 15 inches wide. The floor of the forge is lined with three by four by eight inch fire brick. Each firebrick with each brick has eight holes in if for pumping air into the forge. The front of the forge is open so you can place your work on the burning charcoal or you can burry it in the charcoal. For economy I have a two inch thick ceramic lid that I can place over the top of the forge to hold in heat. It is a little shorter than the forge so hot gasses can escape out the top back.

I may put together a materials list and some blueprints on how all three units are made. Having a friend who does pottery and has a kiln will make the job go a lot easier.
